title: Ocean currents coloured by sea surface temperature
image_description: A flat world map of the ocean's surface currents, drawn as thousands of thin swirling lines. Each line is coloured by the temperature of the water: blue is near 0 degrees C, green is 10 to 20, yellow about 25 and red up to 32 degrees C. The warmest water (orange and red) forms a wide belt along the equator, strongest in the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean. The water cools through green to blue toward both poles, and the coldest band circles Antarctica. You can see warm currents running up the east coasts of the continents, such as the Gulf Stream off North America and the Kuroshio off Japan, and many small swirling eddies. Land is grey and silent. The model is ECCO2 (MIT and JPL), from a NASA visualization released in 2012 covering March 2007 to March 2008.
audio_description:
The sweep lasts 8 seconds and moves from the left edge of the picture to the right edge. The sound moves from your left ear to your right ear with it. On this world map, the left edge is 180 degrees west, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and the right edge is back at the same place, 180 degrees east.
Higher notes mean warmer water. Silence means land.
The marimba plays the northern band, 66 to 23 degrees north. Its highest note comes at about 6.8 seconds, near 127 degrees east (26 degrees C), and its lowest at about 3.8 seconds, near 8 degrees west (15 degrees C). It goes quiet from 1.5 to 1.9 seconds (110 degrees west to 98 degrees west); from 4.9 to 6.6 seconds (42 degrees east to 115 degrees east), where there is land.
The strings play the tropics, 23 north to 23 south. Their highest note comes at about 7.0 seconds, near 138 degrees east (29 degrees C), and their lowest at about 2.0 seconds, near 87 degrees west (24 degrees C). They go quiet from 4.4 to 4.8 seconds (20 degrees east to 31 degrees east), where there is land.
The pluck plays the southern band, 23 to 66 degrees south. Its highest note comes at about 7.6 seconds, near 166 degrees east (13 degrees C), and its lowest at about 2.6 seconds, near 59 degrees west (6 degrees C).
credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio. ECCO2 model (MIT/JPL).
